288.title: The Catholic Church
288.hook: the largest church, united with the Bishop of Rome, with the Mass at its heart
288.howItsDone: Catholics are asked to attend Mass every Sunday and on holy days of obligation, and many also pray the rosary, go to confession, and honor Mary and the saints.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Orthodoxy: icons, incense, and iron glowing in the fire. Your line was heaven on earth. What moment of beauty made you forget where you were? Day two hundred eighty-eight.

Sunday morning moves around the planet. As the sun rises over a village in the Philippines, a bell rings and a priest lifts a round white host. An hour or so later, the same thing in Vietnam. Then in India, in Nigeria, in Poland, in Brazil at a packed six o'clock evening Mass, in a little church in Ohio with forty people and a slightly out-of-tune organ. The languages change. The music changes. In the Latin rite, the words are nearly the same, translated from one Latin book. That's the scale of the church we meet today, the largest Christian church on earth. Today's word is its name.
screen: `THE SUN MOVES AROUND THE WORLD.` → `THE SAME MASS, MANY LANGUAGES.` → `THE LARGEST CHURCH.`

segments.voice: The Catholic Church is the communion of churches united with the bishop of Rome, the pope. Catholics trace that role to Peter, and to Jesus's words to him in Matthew: "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." The name Peter means rock. Catholics understand the pope as Peter's successor, a sign and servant of the church's unity. Other Christians read that verse differently, some saying the rock is Peter's faith, or Christ himself. It's a very old conversation, and it still goes on. At the heart of Catholic life is the Mass. Catholics believe that in the Mass, the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ, and they call the Eucharist the source and summit of the Christian life. The word Mass itself comes from the last Latin line of the old service: ite, missa est, go, it is the dismissal. Missa comes from the verb to send: the service ends by sending people out. Around the Mass sit seven sacraments, from baptism to the anointing of the sick, marking a life from birth to death. And the Catholic Church isn't only Roman. Alongside the large Latin church there are more than twenty Eastern Catholic churches, Ukrainian, Maronite, Melkite, Chaldean and others, with their own liturgies, their own customs, some with married priests, all in communion with the pope. And the word catholic itself means universal, from a Greek phrase, according to the whole. We'll come back to that word later on the path.
screen: `UNITED WITH THE BISHOP OF ROME.` · `THE MASS: SOURCE AND SUMMIT.` · `ITE, MISSA EST: GO, IT IS THE DISMISSAL.` · `NOT ONLY ROMAN: EASTERN CATHOLICS.` · then, large: `UPON THIS ROCK I WILL BUILD MY CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one thing a Catholic friend loves. Settle, and breathe. Think of a Catholic you know, or knew: a grandmother, a coworker, a friend from school. What did they love? Maybe the rosary in their pocket. A saint they talked to. Midnight Mass at Christmas. The smell of the church. Hold that one thing in mind with respect. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for the Catholic Church. If you don't know any Catholics, picture that little church in Ohio, forty people and an out-of-tune organ. The bell holds the time.
Missa. The Latin word the Mass gets its name from, meaning the sending, the dismissal at the end of the service.
Your line: universal. Today, ask a Catholic friend what they love about their church, and just listen. Day two hundred eighty-eight.

289.title: Luther's hammer
289.hook: in 1517 a monk posted 95 theses; he said we're saved by grace through faith
289.howItsDone: Lutheran and some other Protestant churches keep October 31 as Reformation Day, often singing Luther's hymn "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God," and preach on grace, faith and scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Catholic Church, the Mass at its heart, and one word, missa. Your line was universal. Did you hear what a Catholic friend loves? Day two hundred eighty-nine.

October 31, 1517. Wittenberg, a small university town in Germany. A thirty-three-year-old monk and professor named Martin Luther has written ninety-five short arguments, in Latin, against the sale of indulgences: letters people bought believing they would shorten the punishment due for sin in purgatory, for themselves or for loved ones who had died. A preacher named Tetzel was selling them nearby, and people were paying. The story goes that Luther walked to the door of the castle church and nailed the theses up with a hammer. Historians argue about the hammer. What's certain is that he mailed them to his archbishop that same day. He wanted a debate among scholars. Instead, printers copied them, and soon they were spreading across Germany, in German too. He'd started something much bigger than a debate. Today's word is its name.
screen: `WITTENBERG, OCTOBER 31, 1517.` → `NINETY-FIVE THESES.` → `A DEBATE THAT GOT AWAY.`

segments.voice: The Reformation is the name for the movement that began with Luther and reshaped Western Christianity in the 1500s. Reform means to form again, to bring back into shape. Luther didn't set out to start a new church. He wanted to reform the one he belonged to. But under the argument about indulgences lay a question that had tormented him for years. He'd been a desperately serious monk, confessing for hours, never sure he'd done enough to stand before a holy God. Then, reading Paul's letter to the Romans, he fastened on one line, "The just shall live by faith," and he said it felt like the gates of paradise opening. Righteousness wasn't something he had to earn. It was a gift. Ephesians puts it in one sentence: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." From that grew the convictions later summed up in Latin slogans: by grace alone, by faith alone, by scripture alone. Luther translated the Bible into German so ordinary people could read it, and he wrote hymns for whole congregations to sing. The Catholic Church answered at the Council of Trent. Catholics also taught, and teach, that salvation is God's gift of grace, but they understood faith, works and the church's role differently, and the two sides condemned each other. Wars followed, and the West was divided. Centuries later, Catholics and Lutherans have found they agree on more than their ancestors thought. We'll come to that later. For today, just the line that set a monk free.
screen: `REFORM: TO FORM AGAIN.` · `THE JUST SHALL LIVE BY FAITH.` · `BY GRACE, FAITH, AND SCRIPTURE ALONE.` · `TRENT ANSWERS; THE WEST DIVIDES.` · then, large: `FOR BY GRACE ARE YE SAVED THROUGH FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Ephesians 2:8, slowly, three times. For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God. Settle, and breathe. Notice the word gift. Think of something in your life you know you didn't earn: a person, a morning, a second chance. Hold it like a gift, not a wage. If you pray, you can give thanks for grace. If you don't, just rest in the idea that not everything has to be earned. The bell holds the time.
Reformation. The movement, begun by Martin Luther in 1517, to bring the Western church back into shape around grace, faith and scripture.
Your line: by grace, through faith. Today, when you catch yourself trying to earn something that was already given, stop, and just receive it. Day two hundred eighty-nine.

290.title: Lutherans and the Reformed
290.hook: Lutherans kept much liturgy; Calvin's Reformed churches stressed God's sovereignty and scripture
290.howItsDone: Lutheran churches usually worship with a set liturgy, hymns and weekly or frequent communion; Reformed and Presbyterian churches center worship on the reading and preaching of scripture, often in plain sanctuaries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Reformation: a monk, ninety-five theses, and one line from Ephesians. Your line was by grace through faith. What did you catch yourself trying to earn? Day two hundred ninety.

Walk into two Protestant churches from the 1600s. The first is a Lutheran church in Germany. There's an altar with candles, a crucifix, maybe painted panels, a pastor in robes, and up in the balcony an organ roaring out a hymn the whole congregation knows by heart. Johann Sebastian Bach will one day write music for churches like this. The second is a Reformed church in the Netherlands or Scotland. The walls are whitewashed. No statues, no pictures. In the center, instead of an altar, a tall pulpit, and on it an open Bible. The people sing psalms, plainly. It's so bare your eye has nowhere to go but the pulpit. Both came out of the same Reformation, just a few years apart. Today's word is the two families that grew from it.
screen: `CANDLES, CRUCIFIX, AN ORGAN.` → `WHITE WALLS, A PULPIT, A BIBLE.` → `SAME REFORMATION, TWO ROOMS.`

segments.voice: Lutherans follow Martin Luther. His rule of thumb was this: keep whatever in the old worship the Bible doesn't forbid. So Lutherans kept much of the liturgy, the church year, vestments, candles, and they poured their faith into music. Bach, a Lutheran, often wrote three letters at the end of his scores: S.D.G., soli Deo gloria, to God alone the glory. The Reformed tradition comes from Swiss reformers, Ulrich Zwingli in Zurich and, above all, John Calvin in Geneva. Their rule of thumb went further: in worship, keep what scripture calls for, and let the rest go. Hence the white walls. From Geneva, the Reformed faith spread to Scotland, where John Knox founded what became the Presbyterian church, to the Netherlands, Hungary, and later New England. At its center is the sovereignty of God: God is king over everything, every life, every hour, and salvation is God's work from start to finish. A catechism written in 1647 for Reformed churches in England and Scotland opens with a famous question and answer: "What is the chief end of man? Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever." Notice the second half. Enjoy. The two families agreed on almost everything, grace, faith, scripture, but split over communion. At a meeting in Marburg in 1529, Luther and Zwingli agreed on fourteen points out of fifteen. The fifteenth was the Lord's Supper. Luther held that Christ's body is truly present in the bread; Zwingli saw it as a memorial; Calvin later taught a real but spiritual presence. They couldn't agree, and parted. Nearly five centuries later, many Lutheran and Reformed churches signed agreements that put them in full communion, in Europe in 1973 and in the United States in 1997.
screen: `LUTHERANS: KEEP WHAT ISN'T FORBIDDEN.` · `REFORMED: KEEP WHAT SCRIPTURE CALLS FOR.` · `GOD IS KING OVER EVERYTHING.` · `MARBURG: FOURTEEN OF FIFTEEN.` · then, large: `TO GLORIFY GOD, AND TO ENJOY HIM FOR EVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice something simple and beautiful. If you can, picture a church you know: a candle, a window, a plain wooden table, an open Bible. If you're not near a church, look around the room you're in. Find one simple thing that is beautiful exactly as it is. Settle, and breathe. Let it be enough. If you pray, you can give it back with Bach's three letters: to God alone the glory. If you don't, just enjoy it. The catechism would say that counts too. The bell holds the time.
Chief end. The Westminster catechism's phrase for why we exist at all: to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever.
Your line: god is sovereign. Today, when something is out of your control, notice it, and let it be held by someone bigger. Day two hundred ninety.

291.title: Anglicans
291.hook: the Church of England and its worldwide family: a middle way, the Book of Common Prayer
291.howItsDone: Anglicans worship from a prayer book, with set prayers, readings and collects for each Sunday; many churches say Morning and Evening Prayer daily and celebrate Holy Communion weekly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lutherans and the Reformed, and the chief end of man: an organ and candles, white walls and a pulpit. Your line was god is sovereign. What did you let go of that was out of your hands? Day two hundred ninety-one.

These words turn up at weddings, even for people who never set foot in a church: dearly beloved, we are gathered together here. For better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health. And at funerals: earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust. Those lines, give or take a word, come from one book, shaped above all by one man, an archbishop named Thomas Cranmer, in the 1540s and 50s. He was later burned at the stake for his faith. His book taught generations to pray in their own language, and quietly shaped the English language itself. It's called the Book of Common Prayer. Common, as in shared: the same prayers, said together, by everyone. Today's word is the family of churches that grew around it.
screen: `FOR BETTER, FOR WORSE.` → `ASHES TO ASHES.` → `ONE BOOK, PRAYED IN COMMON.`

segments.voice: Anglicans are the Church of England and the worldwide churches that grew from it: the Episcopal Church in the United States, the Church of Nigeria, the Church of Uganda, the Anglican Church of Australia and many more, with large and growing churches in Africa. The break with Rome came under King Henry the Eighth in the 1530s, tangled up with his marriage and his politics as much as with faith. But under Cranmer, and later Queen Elizabeth the First, the church found a shape of its own. Anglicans came to describe it as a middle way: Catholic in its bishops, its creeds and its sacraments; Reformed in its stress on scripture, grace, and worship in the people's own language. Some Anglicans lean toward the Catholic side, with incense and vestments; some toward the evangelical side, with preaching and plain services. They share one book of prayer, in many languages. One small form runs all through the book: the collect. That's COL-lect, stress on the first syllable, a short prayer that gathers up the people's prayers into one sentence. It usually names God, remembers something God has done, asks, and ends through Christ. Here is one said at the start of the communion service, from the 1662 book: "Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open, all desires known, and from whom no secrets are hid: Cleanse the thoughts of our hearts by the inspiration of thy Holy Spirit, that we may perfectly love thee, and worthily magnify thy holy Name; through Christ our Lord. Amen." One sentence. Nothing hidden. That's the Anglican genius: large things said in few, careful words.
screen: `A WORLDWIDE FAMILY, STRONG IN AFRICA.` · `CATHOLIC AND REFORMED: A MIDDLE WAY.` · `THE COLLECT: ONE GATHERING SENTENCE.` · `UNTO WHOM ALL HEARTS BE OPEN.` · then, large: `FROM WHOM NO SECRETS ARE HID.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray a collect, if you pray. Settle, and breathe. Then say the Collect for Purity slowly, one phrase per breath. Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open, all desires known, and from whom no secrets are hid. Stop there, and let that sink in. Nothing hidden. Then, if you wish, the rest. If you don't pray, just sit with the idea of being fully known, and not turned away. The bell holds the time.
Anglicans. The Church of England and its worldwide family, praying from the Book of Common Prayer, walking a middle way.
Your line: a middle way. Today, when you're pulled between two sides, look for the ground where both hold something true. Day two hundred ninety-one.

292.title: Anabaptists
292.hook: Mennonites, Amish, Hutterites: adult baptism, simplicity and nonviolence, at great cost
292.howItsDone: Anabaptist churches baptize those old enough to choose faith, many refuse military service, and communities such as the Amish and Hutterites live simply, share work, and decide together which modern tools to use.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Anglicans: Cranmer's prayer book and the collect. Your line was a middle way. Where did you find ground that both sides could stand on? Day two hundred ninety-two.

The Netherlands, winter, 1569. A man named Dirk Willems has escaped from prison, where he's been held for his faith, and he's running across a frozen pond. A guard is chasing him. Dirk makes it across; the ice holds his thin, starved body. Behind him, the guard crashes through the ice and starts to drown, screaming for help. Dirk is free. Nobody would blame him for running. He stops. He turns around. He goes back across the ice and pulls his pursuer out of the water. The guard wants to let him go, the story says, but the magistrate on the shore orders him taken. Dirk is led back to prison, and soon after he's burned at the stake. His story is kept in a thick old book of martyrs, the Martyrs Mirror, still found in Amish and Mennonite homes. Today's word is his people.
screen: `A FROZEN POND, 1569.` → `HE TURNS BACK.` → `HE SAVES THE MAN CHASING HIM.`

segments.voice: Anabaptists means rebaptizers, from the Greek ana, again. It was a name their enemies gave them. They said they weren't baptizing anyone again: the baptism of a baby, before it could believe, simply wasn't baptism in their eyes. It began in Zurich, in January 1525, when a small group met in a house, and one of them, Conrad Grebel, baptized a former priest, George Blaurock, as an adult who had chosen to follow Christ. It was dangerous. Catholic and Protestant authorities alike treated infant baptism as the glue of society. Within two years, one of that little group, Felix Manz, was drowned in Zurich's river. Many more Anabaptists were executed in the decades that followed. Out of this came families that still live today. The Mennonites, named for Menno Simons, a Dutch former priest. The Amish, who split from the Mennonites in the 1690s under Jakob Ammann. The Hutterites, who share all their property in common. They differ from each other, but they share a few things. Baptism for believers who choose it. A church separate from the state. Simplicity. And nonviolence, taken straight from the Sermon on the Mount: "resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." Many refuse military service, even at great cost. It's why the Amish choose carefully which technology to let in: not because machines are evil, but to protect the life of the community. And it's why a man running for his life turned back on the ice.
screen: `REBAPTIZERS: A NAME FROM ENEMIES.` · `ZURICH, 1525: A CHOSEN BAPTISM.` · `MENNONITES, AMISH, HUTTERITES.` · `SIMPLICITY AND NONVIOLENCE.` · then, large: `TURN TO HIM THE OTHER ALSO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one simple hour. Settle, and breathe. Pick an hour later today, or tomorrow. No screen in it. No buying anything. Maybe a walk, a meal cooked slowly, a conversation, work with your hands. Picture it now, clearly, what you'll do and where. Notice how much quieter it already feels. If you pray, you can offer that hour to God. If you don't, just let it be an hour of peace, for you and anyone near you. The bell holds the time.
Anabaptists. The rebaptizers, a name from their enemies: Mennonites, Amish and Hutterites, who baptize believers and choose simplicity and peace.
Your line: the peaceable way. Today, live simply for one hour, and when someone crosses you, turn back toward them instead of away. Day two hundred ninety-two.

293.title: Baptists and free churches
293.hook: a believer's baptism, a local congregation, freedom of conscience
293.howItsDone: Baptist churches baptize believers by immersion, often in a pool at the front of the church, each congregation calls its own pastor, and worship centers on preaching, singing and prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Anabaptists, and a man who turned back on the ice. Your line was the peaceable way. Did you find your simple hour? Day two hundred ninety-three.

London, 1612. A man named Thomas Helwys has just come home from exile in Amsterdam, where he helped start one of the very first Baptist congregations. Now he's written a little book, and he does something bold. He signs a copy and sends it to King James, the same King James whose name is on the famous Bible. In it, Helwys tells the king, more or less: you are a mortal man, not God. You have no power over people's souls. Let them be heretics, Muslims, Jews or anything else: it isn't the king's business to punish anyone for what they believe. In 1612, that was almost unthinkable. Helwys was thrown into prison, and died there a few years later. Today's word is the family of churches that carried his idea.
screen: `LONDON, 1612.` → `A BOOK SENT TO THE KING.` → `YOU HAVE NO POWER OVER SOULS.`

segments.voice: Baptists began among English Christians in the early 1600s, in exile in Amsterdam, around John Smyth and Thomas Helwys. They held three things close. First, baptism is for believers: people old enough to say for themselves that they follow Christ. Baptists baptize by immersion, all the way under the water, and they love Paul's picture of it: "we are buried with him by baptism into death," and raised to "walk in newness of life." Other churches, Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Reformed, Methodist, baptize infants too, seeing baptism as God's gift before a child can ask for it. Both sides have scripture they cherish, and the conversation goes on. Second, the local congregation. Each Baptist church governs itself; no bishop or king above it. That's what free church means: free from the state, free to call its own pastor. Many other churches share that shape: Congregationalists, Churches of Christ, countless independent churches. Third, freedom of conscience, which Baptists sometimes call soul freedom or soul liberty. For Baptists, faith can't be forced. It has to be chosen, freely, or it isn't faith. Roger Williams, who founded Providence, in what became Rhode Island, in 1636, built a colony on that principle, and helped start a Baptist church there, remembered as the first in America. Baptists pushed hard for the separation of church and state in the new United States. Black Baptist churches were at the heart of the civil rights movement: Martin Luther King Jr. was a Baptist pastor. From a book sent to a king in 1612 to a pulpit in Montgomery, one idea: nobody can believe for you.
screen: `BAPTISM FOR THOSE WHO CHOOSE IT.` · `A FREE, LOCAL CONGREGATION.` · `SOUL FREEDOM: FAITH CAN'T BE FORCED.` · `FROM RHODE ISLAND TO MONTGOMERY.` · then, large: `WALK IN NEWNESS OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be thankful for freedom of conscience. Settle, and breathe. Think of what you believe, or don't, today. Notice that you're free to hold it, free to question it, free to be right here learning. Many people in history weren't. Some still aren't. If you pray, you can thank God for freedom of conscience, and pray for those who are in prison for what they believe. If you don't, just let yourself feel grateful for the freedom, and hold those people in mind. The bell holds the time.
Baptists and free churches. Believers' baptism, self-governing congregations, and freedom of conscience for everyone.
Your line: soul freedom. Today, when you meet someone who believes differently from you, let them be free, and notice how it feels to give that freedom. Day two hundred ninety-three.

294.title: Methodists
294.hook: John Wesley felt his heart strangely warmed (1738), and societies spread by horseback
294.howItsDone: Methodists sing the Wesleys' hymns, many meet in small groups for prayer and accountability, and many Methodist churches celebrate Aldersgate Day on May 24.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baptists and free churches, and a letter to a king. Your line was soul freedom. Who did you let be free to believe differently? Day two hundred ninety-four.

London, the evening of May 24, 1738. A small, tired Anglican priest named John Wesley goes, in his own words, very unwillingly, to a meeting in a room on Aldersgate Street. He's thirty-four. He's just come back from a mission to Georgia that went badly. He's been fasting, praying, working, and still feels no peace. Someone at the meeting is reading aloud from Martin Luther's preface to Paul's letter to the Romans. Nothing dramatic. No music. Just someone reading. And at about a quarter to nine, as he later wrote in his journal, while the reader was describing the change God works in the heart through faith, "I felt my heart strangely warmed." Today's word is the movement that grew from that warmth.
screen: `ALDERSGATE STREET, 1738.` → `SOMEONE READS LUTHER ON ROMANS.` → `A QUARTER TO NINE.`

segments.voice: Methodist started as a joke. At Oxford, John Wesley, his brother Charles and a few friends had formed a little club that prayed, studied, fasted and visited prisoners on a strict schedule. Other students mocked them as Methodists, for their method. The name stuck. After Aldersgate, Wesley took his warmed heart outdoors. When churches closed their pulpits to him, he preached in fields, to coal miners at dawn with their faces black with soot. He spent decades on horseback, preaching wherever people would gather. He organized people into small groups, called classes, that met weekly and asked each other one simple question: how is it with your soul? His brother Charles wrote a great many hymns, among them Hark! the Herald Angels Sing. Wesley taught that God's grace doesn't only forgive; it changes you, and can grow a whole life toward love. He called it holiness of heart and life, and it spilled over into schools, clinics and the fight against slavery. In America, circuit riders carried Methodism across the frontier on horseback. Wesley lived and died an Anglican priest. Methodists became their own churches after him. There's an echo here of the road to Emmaus: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" A heart warmed while someone opened the scriptures. And look back at this week: the Catholic Church; Luther's hammer; Lutherans and the Reformed; Anglicans; Anabaptists; Baptists; and now the Methodists. Seven days, each lit by something.
screen: `METHODIST: A JOKE ABOUT A METHOD.` · `FIELDS, MINERS, A HORSE.` · `HOW IS IT WITH YOUR SOUL?` · `GRACE THAT CHANGES A LIFE.` · then, large: `I FELT MY HEART STRANGELY WARMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice your heart warming. Settle, and breathe, with a hand on your chest if you like. Think of a moment when something unexpected moved you: a line in a song, a kindness from a stranger, words read aloud. Let it come back. Notice where you feel it in your body. Then ask Wesley's class question, quietly, of yourself: how is it with your soul? No need to answer quickly. If you pray, you can ask God to warm your heart. If you don't, just listen for the answer. The bell holds the time.
Methodists. The movement of John and Charles Wesley: a warmed heart, small groups, hymns, and grace that changes a life.
Your line: strangely warmed. Today, ask one person Wesley's question, in your own words: how are you, really? And listen. Day two hundred ninety-four.
